The core idea is right: Twitter timelines are traversed by tweet ID, not page number. The v2 docs list 'Traversing timelines by Post IDs' and 'retrieve new results since the since_id' as shared by v1.1 and v2. since_id only fetches tweets newer than an ID. The syntax is right. Missing: LIMIT/OFFSET pages are only stable with an ORDER BY that gives a unique order. PostgreSQL warns that different LIMIT/OFFSET values 'will give inconsistent results unless you enforce a predictable result ordering with ORDER BY'. MySQL says rows with identical ORDER BY values may come back in any order, and that the order can depend on LIMIT.
precise_version: Limit-offset: SELECT ... WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0, then OFFSET 10, 20 ...; without a unique ORDER BY the pages are not stable.

note: Correct. PostgreSQL: 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.' MongoDB: 'As the offset increases, skip() will become slower.'

This is right for the common engines: PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Elasticsearch docs all say deep offsets are costly, and that seek/range queries are the fix. 'Literally every database' over-generalises. How much offset costs and how much keyset helps depend on the engine and on whether an index matches the sort.
Correct. MongoDB documents skip()+limit() pagination: 'The skip() method requires the server to scan from the beginning of the input results set before beginning to return results.'
Correct. PostgreSQL: skipped rows 'still have to be computed inside the server'. MongoDB: skip scans from the beginning of the result set. Each page repeats that work, so cost grows with the offset.

Keyset (ID-based) pagination is not limited to plain table iteration. It works with WHERE filters and other sort orders when an index matches the filter plus sort columns, e.g. an index on (sale_date, sale_id) with a row-values predicate. Its real limits are a deterministic sort order and no jumping to arbitrary pages.
An illustrative claim about Twitter's internal batch workloads; no public source describes them this way. Technically harmless: keyset pagination suits sequential scans of a time-ordered ID range.

Right that these IDs are comparable. Missing: MongoDB says ObjectIds are 'approximately ordered by creation time, but are not perfectly ordered' (one-second resolution, client clocks). Snowflake promises only k-sorted IDs 'within a reasonable bound (we're promising 1s...)'. So when you iterate 'the last N minutes', a row with a slightly smaller ID can appear after you have passed its position.
precise_version: ID-limit pagination needs comparable IDs; auto-increment, ObjectId and Snowflake IDs all compare, though time-based IDs are only roughly time-ordered.

note: The pattern is right, but the query must also sort on the key, or the 'next 10' are not guaranteed to be the next 10 by ID. MongoDB's own example is find({_id: {$lt: startValue}}).sort({_id: -1}).limit(n), and SQL needs ORDER BY id.
precise_version: db.students.find({_id: {$gt: lastId}}).sort({_id: 1}).limit(10) (SQL: WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 10), repeated with the last id seen.

note: Only some engines physically store rows in primary-key order. MySQL InnoDB does: 'the clustered index ... stores row data' and is the primary key. PostgreSQL tables are heaps: CLUSTER 'is a one-time operation' and new rows are not kept in index order. A normal MongoDB collection 'stores the _id index separately from the documents' (clustered collections are an opt-in since 5.3). ID pagination is fast because an index on the key lets the query seek straight to the last ID, not because the data itself is stored in order.
precise_version: ID-limit pagination is efficient because an index on the ID (in InnoDB, the clustered primary key) lets the database seek directly to the last ID and read the next rows in order, so cost does not grow with depth.

note: The teacher's blog benchmark agrees: 'The approach using _id and limit almost gives constant performance and is independent of size of the result set' and 'till 500-600 count, both the approaches are comparable'. The 'linear' description of skip-limit comes from the on-screen graph; the blog text describes a rise past a threshold.

This exactly describes an InnoDB clustered primary key, whose leaf pages hold the rows. In heap-based stores (PostgreSQL, non-clustered MongoDB) the database does an index range scan, then fetches each row: still roughly constant per page, but not one sequential scan of the data. 'Does not increase' is approximate, since log n grows slowly with table size.

Keyset pagination does work with WHERE filters and other sort orders: use a deterministic sort key (e.g. (sale_date, sale_id)), a row-values predicate on the last values seen, and an index that matches filter plus sort. The real costs are that 'you also cannot fetch arbitrary pages' and that you need a fitting index. Offset is still needed for jump-to-page-N UIs, and for filters or sorts that no index matches.
precise_version: Disadvantage of ID/keyset pagination: you cannot jump to an arbitrary page, and it needs a deterministic sort key with an index covering the filter and sort; queries that do not fit an index still fall back to offset.

note: The advice is sound (use keyset for deep iteration, don't rewrite everything). The stated reason is too strong: see L-0234. Keyset does handle WHERE clauses when an index matches the filter and sort columns.

'Depends on the storage engine' is right. In MongoDB it works through the _id index, even though a normal collection is not physically ordered by _id (see L-0229).

The data-locality point holds for range scans. But hash-partitioned stores still give efficient cursor pagination. A DynamoDB Query reads one partition key's items in sort-key order and pages with LastEvaluatedKey -> ExclusiveStartKey, never with an offset. What you lose with hash placement is a cheap globally ordered range scan across partitions, not cursor pagination itself.
precise_version: Keyset/cursor pagination is efficient wherever the store can resume a scan from a key (B-tree tables, DynamoDB sort keys); hash-distributed layouts lose cheap global ordered ranges, not cursors.

note: The 10,000 figure is right, but it is a default, not a hard-coded limit: 'By default, you cannot use from and size to page through more than 10,000 hits. This limit is a safeguard set by the index.max_result_window index setting.' The parameters are from/size, not offset. For deeper pages Elastic recommends search_after (with a point in time), and says 'We no longer recommend using the scroll API for deep pagination' (current Elasticsearch docs, checked Oct 2026).
precise_version: Elasticsearch's from/size pagination is capped by default at 10,000 hits (index.max_result_window); beyond that use search_after with a point in time.

note: Correct. Elastic: 'If you need to page through more than 10,000 hits, use the search_after parameter instead.'

String keys are comparable, but the order follows the column's collation, not plain bytes. MySQL: 'A collation is a set of rules for comparing characters', and case-insensitive collations treat 'a' and 'A' as equal. Numeric strings also sort lexicographically ('10' < '9'), so string IDs page correctly only if their sort order is the order you want (e.g. fixed-width or zero-padded).
